utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Dr. Marina Lostal, who holds a PhD from the University of Cambridge in international humanitarian law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just begin with one omission that I missed yesterday, Your Honours. And that was to request that pages 30 in English and 31 in B/C/S of 65 ter number 25898. If you recall, that was the appellate verdict in the case against Marko Samardzija that we discussed yesterday and I had made the mistake of not identifying B/C/S pages. I wonder if those pages that we referred to in court could be tendered as Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, last night I read your evidence from yesterday and your comments about some of the documents that I was showing you, so I just want to be clear now if I understand your position correctly. It's your evidence that on July 9th and 10th, 1992, you were not the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade; right? That's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had no responsibility, command or otherwise, for any aspect of the operation at Biljani on those days; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any command responsibility. Well, in part it can be understood that it was there because I was present in some areas, but I didn't have any command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We may come back to that, but I'll just go through your evidence from yesterday first. You weren't Marko Samardzija's superior. You said that yesterday. That's your evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If being a superior is understood as being a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, could you stop and repeat what you were just saying because the interpreter didn't understand the words you used.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Marko Samardzija participated in the forming of the unit as the unit was set up and recruited. Another man took up the position of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm focusing on the 9th and 10th of July, 1992. And your evidence is you didn't and you couldn't know anything about the killings and abuses that happened at the primary school, in particular on the morning of the 10th? That's what you said yesterday; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'll try it another way. Your evidence with respect to the morning of the 10th of July, 1992, is that your contact with Samardzija was limited to telling him that when his men finished their assignment of gathering the Muslim men, and the civilian and military security people arrived, they could go home. That's your evidence; right? That's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Samardzija never told you anything strange was happening at the primary school. He never reported anything was afoot, not in your radio contact, and not when he later reported to you at the station; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Marko Samardzija in the evening of that day, when news reached us that there had been killings. Our conversation had to do with that. We didn't know how many people were killed nor how it came about. Marko did not submit a typical classic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your written evidence at paragraph 9 that individuals and groups that you don't know broke free of army and police control and raided the school and the yard and killed Muslims, you actually really don't know. Based on what you've just said, that's just speculation; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What comes out of this sort of information is that there were groups active throughout the territory, roaming if I can say it, engaging in criminal activities, plundering whatever came within their reach, regardless of the ethnicity. They were simply groups prepared to do any sort of ill-deeds. So at a later date, we found out that it was about these groups who broke free of control and burst into that area at some point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you don't know because you said it in your evidence who they were. It's just speculation; right? Your evidence -- let's do it this way: Your evidence is you don't know who was on the scene at the primary school; right? You don't know.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you mean. Who was -- what do you mean: Who was in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. You don't know who was there at the primary school from the civilian police, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know who was there at the primary school from the military police, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know who was there at the primary school from the reconnaissance platoon, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify which reconnaissance platoon you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why do I need to do that? Do you know or don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the establishment of the battalion, there was no reconnaissance platoon, if that's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know who was guarding the prisoners at Biljani, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know what orders they would have had then, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for the usual ones, I could only speculate. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know who broke free, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but later on through conversations, I am now able to mention two or three groups, but I don't know who they consisted of or what their official name was. One was Osa, Zolja, and the other one was Bicko or Micko, or something like that. But it was not really established. It was simply information that was circulated later on through various stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am not talking about various stories. I am not talking about random groups who were roaming through the area. I am talking about the people who you say broke free and perpetrated the killings at Biljani. You don't know who they are, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, actually, really, you don't know anything about what happened at Biljani on the morning of the 10th of July, 1992; right? Anything you say about it is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please don't. I know that people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unarmed people; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim men who were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now just to move on, I want to ask you something about another couple of locations we were talking about yesterday: Prhovo and Peci. Do you agree that civilians were killed at Prhovo and Peci at the end of May and the beginning of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered this question of yours, and I now confirm that I truly am not aware of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So since you're not aware of these cases and since you told us yesterday you and your unit weren't even there at that time, your comments in paragraphs 15 to 22 of your statement about the events in Pudin Han and Prhovo are also just speculation; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the fact of whether I had that information contemporaneously or learned about it later on, then you're right. I only came to know about these things later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also said in your statement at paragraph 9, talking about Biljani, that investigating authorities came from Banja Luka and arrested whoever they could, and as far as you knew these people were taken to Banja Luka and proceedings were conducted against them. That's also speculation - right? - because you don't even know who they are?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, if the fact that I received information at a later date amounts to speculation, then I don't know what to say. We heard that certain people, groups participating in these crimes, were arrested and were taken into custody by these security organs and transferred to Banja Luka. There is another thing that I didn't mention there. It seems to me that on the following day, one of the security organs by the name of Tomic, a refugee from either Bihac or Sarajevo, came to Kosanica, because he had some business of his there, and he told me in passing, We are about to capture two more people. Whether they did arrest them or not, I don't know, but this means that even after these criminals were arrested, this action continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just stick with your assertion that investigating authorities detained people and instituted proceedings against the people who were responsible for the killings at Biljani. If you know, then, who are the people? Where are the files? Where is the register of those proceedings? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, let's make this clear. At the level of the battalion, no such records are kept and there is no obligation on the part of anyone to send this information to battalions. The procedure of investigative organs, especially those in the military and with the security organ, when it comes to the police and security services this procedure ends at the local municipal level as well as at higher up. In other words, in addition to the judiciary, this sort of information would also be sent to these organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that this Court has heard from Dr. Karadzic's own Defence witnesses that throughout the whole war the military court in Banja Luka only ever instituted proceedings for war crimes against civilians in one case and this wasn't the one, so, Mr. Kevac, what you are talking about? What proceedings are you talking about in your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hesitate to use this sentence, but I have to: Please, when you're putting your question, can you refer to the situation at hand. I was talking about the documentation of the people arrested, and I said that the battalion does not keep any records of those arrested. The investigative bodies which are engaged in investigations do not have a duty to send the information either. I was talking about military security organs. And as for the police, I know -- I happen to know that this is the level of public security stations, the lower level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt here. Probably, Mr. Kevac, you didn't understand the question. Shall we upload his statement, Mr. Kevac's statement, paragraph 9. Do you have your statement with you now, your statement given to Mr. Karadzic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not here, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's in front of you. Paragraph 9, second paragraph. That last part: "After this incident, investigating authorities came from Banja Luka and conducted an on-site investigation. They also arrested whoever they could go hold of, and as far as I know these people were taken to Banja Luka and proceedings were conducted against them." So where are the documents of this? If you say so, there should be some documents. Who did you hear this from and on what basis are you saying this? That's the crux of the question of Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is information which was obtained later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from people who were initially there and then returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So please be specific in answering the question of Ms. Edgerton. Who did you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How shall I put it? From soldiers, people, civilians. This was all happening later. It wasn't about me reporting this to -- about somebody reporting this to me or about me seeking information from anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no names to give us and you have no documents supporting your assertion; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now your written evidence in paragraphs 4 to 7 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just before I finish the question, Your Honours, I note I'm just about at the end of my time for cross-examination. I'd ask your indulgence for about another 7 to 10 minutes, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraphs 4 to 7 of your written evidence, you talk about the situation in Kljuc and you say that it was quiet until what you describe as the first incidents. So those are incidents -- the incidents you see in paragraphs 4 to 7. Now those incidents that you list happened on the 25th and 27th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two key incidents, if I can put it that way. However, that first one happened far earlier, as well as the other one related to the relay. I don't know which paragraph that is, the capture of young soldiers and the shutting down of the relay. These incidents happened before the two key incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The incident in paragraph 4 happened on the 25th of May, 1992, Mr. Kevac, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with respect to the ones where you are sure of the date, you didn't put that you knew that and you didn't say that in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just told us you've just confirmed that the -- if I could just have a look at your exact words. The two key incidents that you talk about in your statement, the incidents you describe as key, happen on 27 May, 1992. So you knew that but you didn't say that in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I didn't state the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that an omission or I simply didn't mention it? I can't give you a reason. Probably as I was giving the answer, I didn't pay attention to that element.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. We'll go on to one final area and it's at paragraph 13 of your statement, where you say -- where you make a categorical statement that the policy pursued by the SDS and the military authorities of Kljuc never planned or ordered that Kljuc should be ethnically cleansed and the non-Serbs forced to leave. I want to show you, with respect to that comment of yours, a clip from a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter number 40138C. And it's going to be played in Sanction. I should note for the record that this is a video of two minutes in length and the first minute is part of P6552.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The situation in Kljuc municipality is very complicated." The interpreter cannot find this passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we can stop, begin again, and turn the volume up as well, please, to my friends in the audio booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We found it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The political security situation in the Kljuc municipality is quite complicated. We feel free to say that in the last ten days, the situation has improved somewhat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we -- are we supposed to watch some clips, video-clips?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One two-minute clip, Your Honours. Do you not have it on your computer monitor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand that this is something that our colleagues in the audio booth, because we're playing this in Sanction, should be attending to to make it available to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are our friends in the audio booth able to deal with the fact that the Bench -- neither the Bench nor the witness is able to see this in Sanction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem and they are working on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, keeping in mind efficiency and the effective use of time, this would be my last question. So we could take a breather for a few seconds while they are working on it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, can I say this: Yesterday the Chamber asked the parties for their position as to whether Mr. Mico Stanisic, who is scheduled to testify next week, should be led live due to his position and the fact that he was subpoenaed. The Chamber considered the parties' arguments, examined the statement submitted by the accused, and decided to allow the accused to present Mr. Stanisic's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. This decision was communicated to the parties via e-mail yesterday. Further, the Chamber grants the request for presence of Defence counsel, Mico Stanisic, which was filed on the 29th of January, 2014, and allows counsel for Mico Stanisic to be present in the courtroom for the duration of Mr. Stanisic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We better take a short break for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, we can go straight to the video. And just so my friends, the interpreters, know, we are starting a few lines down in the transcript from where we started before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let me ask you frankly: Do you think that it is possible after all these events that Muslims and Serbs should live together in the area of your municipality? "Generally, it's difficult to answer this question. I mean, how do you assess such a matter? I think that life has to be totally ethnically demarcated and the areas ethnically cleansed of all those who cannot live together in this area."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the witness isn't getting any sound. He's making gestures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, do you hear the sound? Shall we play --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: His volume needs to be turned up because mine was also very low when we commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we repeat. Shall we play from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let me ask you, frankly: Do you think that after all these events it's possible that Serbs and Muslims should live together in the area of your municipality? "Generally speaking, it's difficult to answer this question. I mean, how do you assess such a matter? I think that life has to be totally ethnically demarcated and the areas ethnically cleansed of all those who cannot live together in this area. "Well, is this better done by war or peacefully? "In my opinion, the only solution should be peaceful, never by war. I think that we have not much influence on this in small communities like Kljuc. I think that the leadership at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, together with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, have to do this job, and we will do on that level, to the level of municipalities belonging to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. "If I understood you correctly, this means that it is up to Karadzic in the first place, that the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to find a solution in talks with Alija Izetbegovic, with Boban, in this case with Izetbegovic because it concerns the Muslims of your municipality. "I think that this is the only solution. If this solution is not achieved soon, I'm afraid that we will have to get into an even more difficult situation because the war is not over yet. The war goes on and can easily turn into a war up to the extinction of one or the other side, one or the other people."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, you recognised Jovo Banjac in that video-clip, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you for this opportunity to see the late president even in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Jovo Banjac, who was the president of the Crisis Staff -- of the SDS Crisis Staff in Kljuc municipality, so the highest -- during its existence, the highest organ of government on the territory of the municipality is clearly saying that ethnic separation is the only solution. So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask that we be clear. Is the Crisis Staff of the SDS referred to or the Crisis Staff at the level of the municipality as an authority? And reading should be fair and accurate to avoid misleading and to avoid leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with leading questions, but clarification may be appropriate. Could you clarify with the witness as to the SDS and the exact reference, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, it's correct, isn't it, that Jovo Banjac was the president of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the president, he was also the president of the Crisis Staff in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So here's the man who is the president of the highest organ of government on the territory of Kljuc municipality clearly saying that ethnic separation is the only solution, clearly saying that that's a policy. So when you said --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I am not objecting to leading questions, but I'm objecting to a misleading question. Could we please read exactly what late Mr. Banjac said, who should be separated: Those who cannot live together, who are fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the passage. You have the transcript with you, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm happy to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Banjac was asked, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Kevac: Let me ask you frankly, do you that it's possible that after all these events that Muslims and Serbs live together in the area of your municipality? And, Mr. Kevac and Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Banjac said: "I think that life has to be totally ethnically demarcated and the areas ethnically cleansed of all those who cannot live together in the area". And at the end of that clip we saw, he said: I think that this is the only solution, that that has to be achieved through the intervention of Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, the leaders. So my question, if I can go back to my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where did he say this is the only option? He said only solution would be peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll go further with your leave, Mr. President: "In my opinion," he said, "the only solution would be peaceful, never by war. I think that we have not much influence in these small communities like Kljuc. I think that the leadership on the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina together with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, have to do this job, and we will all on that level, to the level of the municipalities belonging to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And then he was asked: "If he understands you correctly, this means that it is up to Karadzic in the first place, then the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to find a solution in talks with Alija Izetbegovic, with Boban, in this case with Izetbegovic because it concerns the Muslims of your municipality. I think that this is the only solution. If this solution is not achieved soon, I am afraid that we will get into an even more difficult situation because the war is not over yet. The war goes on and can easily turn into a war up to the extinction of one or the other people." I've now read the transcript of that clip verbatim as I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to put your question again? Or, Mr. Kevac, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this preamble, Madam addressed Mr. Karadzic and me both. I don't know who is supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, she referred to Mr. Karadzic as he raised an objection. Please put your question again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this, Mr. Kevac, is a clear illustration that ethnic separation was one of the objectives of the Serbian leaders in Kljuc municipality. That's -- that means that when you categorically denied that as a policy, you were wrong, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to know the time when this was filmed to compare it with the situation on the ground. In your question, you stressed this bit rather than the later passage when it is said that it should be done peacefully. But we see here a man who is burdened with many problems he has to deal with. I read this more as a warning and a suggestion of different ways the situation should be solved and situations that could get more serious and more difficult. But it's important to know the time. Is this April, May, June?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further in cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies. But I wonder, when do you wish to take the break? You had a break and I am at your disposal. I can begin, but then we will have to stop for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll consult my colleagues, but I am minded to take a break after your re-examination is over.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'll need at least 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the break we had earlier on, there should be no problem with that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kevac, you saw a part of one transcript and one video-clip and heard the personal opinion of one of the participants. So I'd like to ask you: What was the thinking and the general attitude towards the Muslim population? Was there a distinction made between the population as a whole and the extremists who had taken up arms?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, Mr. President, you've already provided the answer. Knowing Mr. Banjac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you follow why Ms. Edgerton was on her feet?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you something that the Prosecution hasn't shown us from this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please look at the Serbian and English page 2 of this document, 65 ter 40138, and then page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, look at what Mr. Kondic says at 22 minutes: "Negotiations were held with the most extreme faction and the reply was that they did not wish civilian victims, but they wouldn't give up at any cost, and they'd rather die in battle then hand in their weapons. This is the most extremist faction that I'm talking about, the faction that is so close, so tight knit, and which actually provides a true picture of Muslim fundamentalism." What would you say about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this: The whole psychosis of the war and all that was going on had pervaded everyone, but the leadership of the municipality tried everything possible to keep peace everywhere. Nevertheless, these extremists always posed a danger - I'm speaking slowly for the sake of the interpreters, but I could speak faster - they were trying to secure peace the best they could, but the extremists were a problem not only for the leadership but for their own people. The general conclusion is this: Knowing the personalities involved in that political and organisational leadership of the municipality, especially the late president who was, above all, a humanist and well loved by everyone, all the efforts were focused on keeping peace regardless of who we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says in the last paragraph that they had set an ultimatum with dead-lines and that the Muslim side, the extremists --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move to the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Muslim extremists had prohibited their civilians from moving out of the combat zone and even ordered them to stay there exposed to fire. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, this is about, as we see on the page that was -- that's displayed in front of us, this is about Prhovo, Peci, Pudin Han, Velagici, places that the witness has even given evidence today that he doesn't know anything about and he wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not a valid objection if a witness is giving evidence about things -- and he's answering questions. The fact that he may or may not have answered her questions in a way in which he said he had knowledge of those things doesn't mean that it can't be inquired of. So I don't understand the basis for an objection that he's -- since he already said that he didn't know anything about it therefore he can't be asked any questions, particularly when those questions go to the attitude of the leadership in Kljuc which was directly implicated by her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how does this part of question arise from the line of cross-examination, as it is related to Prhovo and those areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what areas it's related to. The clip that she showed and the questions that she asked were trying to show that the leadership of Kljuc wanted to expel all Muslims from Kljuc. Dr. Karadzic is trying to show that they were talking about the extremists who were engaged in battle and were engaged in activities that allowed them to be arrested, and so that's the point and not whether we are talking about a particular village within Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The basis that this part is also contained in that video footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, although even if it wasn't, I think the topic is engaged by her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you agree this part is part of the larger footage which contains the clip you showed us?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a very lengthy piece of film, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. We'll allow the accused to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your experience is and knowledge as to how the Muslim extremists treated their own population who intended to escape to areas out of direct danger?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of two cases, and I can confirm here that as units came back for short periods of rest, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I would engage in individual conversations with the leaders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How does that arise from the cross-examination, either from the video-clip or any of the other topics I've raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire picture that the Prosecution wants to paint is that the Serbian authorities in Kljuc treated the Muslim population indiscriminately in the sense that it -- the treatment was hostile and contributed to the harm that came to the population. However, the -- there is evidence that the events unfolded quite differently and it arises from the same footage. If the Trial Chamber should believe it could be of assistance, we would suggest that the entire document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this part we agree with Ms. Edgerton. Your question has become very leading. Please move on to another topic. This part Ms. Edgerton showed us was not admitted and we also have sufficient transcript. I think we covered it sufficiently, please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 4 in English and Serbian instead, where localities are mentioned and let's see what happened there. Some of these localities were mentioned by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the previous page, it reads: "Many houses were destroyed. The population fled these villages." And then at the top it goes on to say there were many prisoners. Even the newly built mosque which had yet to be consecrated was destroyed, yet the Serbian army and the police only targeted the houses and buildings from which there was resistance. The new mosque of Alagic's and the one in Pudin Han was one of the strongest Muslim strongholds. The peace that the Serbs offered to the Muslims was rejected in Krasulje, Gornji and Donji Sanica, Plamenica, Prhovo, Ramici, and Kamitcka [phoen]; is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's just one massive leading question. That's just completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me put my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it the case that in the villages mentioned by the Prosecution, there was civilian population unarmed, there were no fortifications, and there was no cause for attack?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it simply: In my earlier answer, I wanted to stress the two localities that I was personally aware of, namely Kamicak, which belongs to Kljuc but is on the border of the municipality of Sanski Most, and Sanica. In all of these localities, including Plamenice, all of these inhabitants went to Kljuc fearing these extremists. And, in fact, I would have nothing to add to what has been stated here in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there were Muslim settlements whose authorities approached the matter differently and where there were no war activities, there was no destruction?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such settlements. I suppose that you're referring to the villages with a Muslim majority, and I can mention two of those; Namely, Zgon and very well Velecevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And actually, Your Honours, to come back to the point we were discussing earlier with respect to these localities, to go any further down that road is kind of assuming facts not in evidence when the witness denied knowledge of anything that had gone on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are of the view that the question was permissible. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zgon and Velecevo. Can you look at the next passage at 27 minutes. It reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The fact that Ms. Edgerton showed a small part of this whole video, does not open the door for you to go through every and each part of the document. You should put your question which should arise from the line of cross, and you can then put some part of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- I think that's exactly what he's done. He's asked whether or not there were Muslim settlements that were -- approached the matter differently where there were no war activities, and what was the situation in those places within the municipality. This goes directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he confirmed that and then he enumerates some names of the village or municipality. Why does he have to show this part again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if there are parts of this that the witness can comment on that go to that topic which is considered to be within the scope of the cross-examination, there is nothing wrong with that. Not only would we have the witness's own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If that's the way in which he wants to spend his time, we have no difficulty. Is that -- please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw that villages were mentioned where there was fighting. Can you look at this passage and can you confirm that this was not the case in Sehici because Sehici was a majority Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was a satellite of the town of Kljuc, just as was the case with Egrlici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Velecevo, Dubocanin, and Zgon? As it reads here, they were exclusively populated by the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could even say that the Muslim population was more than 99 per cent. There may have been an odd Serb household there but very few. Yes, you could say that they were Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they attacked by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These locations were not attacked by Serb forces. I'm afraid, lest the Prosecutor should intervene, there was this incident related to the village of Sehovici where they responded by putting out white sheets in order to avoid that their village should come under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the significance of this piece of cloth?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in films or elsewhere this symbolised a surrender. Our understanding was that they were telling us that we should not be targeting them because they were saying we are peaceful and have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a commander, did you have any particular markings for your own unit to avoid friendly fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Normally these marks were worn on the sleeves and on the shoulder, on the epaulette. We had pieces of cloth of different colour and they varied from period to period for understandable reasons of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution suggested that these were mostly civilians; for instance, in Sanica. What were the clothes that they were wearing? Can you tell us? And how -- what was the insignia worn by the fighters? Could they be distinguished from civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, it was very difficult because on both sides the equipment was of the olive-drab colour that was used by the former JNA. I would like to particularly emphasise the dangerous situations when it came to identification, because certain individuals would only wear parts of uniform. They would have, for instance, a military shirt and the rest would be civilian clothes; or, inversely, they would be wearing only military trousers. In the context of your question, this constituted not just a difficulty for unit commands including the police, understandably, but also for the civilians, for the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how the authorities treated reputable Muslims living in Kljuc who did not engage in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply in a friendly manner. And let me cite the late Banjac here because he was great friends with them. And if this makes any difference, I will mention one name, Dr. Suad Hadzic, a versatile, educated man, free of any prejudice. Every meeting he had with Mr. Banjac would start with hugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 8 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top, 38:10, Ljuban Bajic, a member of the Crisis Staff is speaking, and he was asked this: "At the same time they say that the Muslims in Kljuc were killed?" His answer is this: "These are lies as well. You can see for yourself. If you can, try and come to see the homes of these reputable Muslims. You can talk to them and you will see for yourself that these are outright lies, that there can be no talk of any massacres, imprisonment, killing of Muslims in the Kljuc municipality." How does this accord with your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would confirm this and say this: I was mobilised quite early on and came to learn this when I returned to Kljuc for a short period of rest, but I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the name of Emir Kapetanovic familiar to you and what is the person's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to think back if this is Dr. Emir Kapetanovic. If that is the man, he was a gynecologist, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he stay behind in Kljuc and how was he treated?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that initially he was treated properly, but, believe me, I can't set a time-frame on that or say anything else. I know that initially everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 14 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is just about the manner of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- of going through this transcript is -- I didn't stand up the last time on this, but could I respectfully request Dr. Karadzic be encouraged to ask his question and not treat this as an examination-in-chief and lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So collapse the document first. Could you put your question first that arises from the line of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The suggestion was made on cross-examination that the Serbian side had an indiscriminately hostile approach to the Muslims. I asked the witness if he knew Emir Kapetanovic, I didn't even mention his profession. He said that if that was the gynecologist, then that he -- then he knew him, and he also said that he was able to continue living and working in Kljuc. This same Emir Kapetanovic gave a statement in that programme we were looking at, and I just wanted to ask the witness if this was consistent with his knowledge. Emir Kapetanovic was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Continue. Page 14 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the top. It says: "My practice, I'm a gynecologist by profession, my practice was out of town. I moved there by a combination of circumstances because I could not afford to pay the rent in the town. You know how high the rents there were. It was the war zone and the zone of operations and, alas, it was hit. The practice does not exist anymore. They told me later to go to SUP to report the damage, which is only natural, the same as all the other citizens were." So what is your experience with what became of the Muslims in town, whose property was damaged, and how they were treated as individuals, as persons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about this specific case, but I can confirm by way of a similar case where a proper approach was taken and compensation given. This had to do with the home of another doctor, a dentist whose apartment was damaged. It was in an apartment bloc. His name was Omer Zupcevic, unless I'm mistaken. He was given compensation -- or, in fact, I think the doors and windows of his flat were repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that links with Banja Luka and Prijedor were burned. Is that true? What kind of connection did you have with Pale, if any? Were you able to communicate with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did Ms. Edgerton cover that in her cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, your Excellency, that Ms. Edgerton challenged the non-existence of these links, but I can't cite a reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right because there wasn't one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But also, Mr. President, in the clip which she played, she attempted to link the events in Kljuc and what occurred afterwards to the policies of Dr. Karadzic as mentioned by the president of the Crisis Staff during -- or -- during the question to him, so I think that Dr. Karadzic is entitled to show that his policies did not include this kind of conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how is it related to any kind of connection between Pale and Kljuc at the time -- or Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do you remember in the video-clip when the president of the municipality was asked: Well, would this after then be dealt with by Dr. Karadzic in negotiations? So we think that showing what instructions Dr. Karadzic had given and whether they were followed or even communicated in this municipality would be relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, did you challenge the non-existence of those links?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't raise it all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You didn't raise it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It didn't arise from the line of the cross. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If the Chamber finds it useful, we will tender this entire video-clip and the transcript. I believe it could do no harm to anybody. I tender them, in fact. 65 ter 40138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would think only those specific pages that Dr. Karadzic dealt with with the witness. Also, I didn't even tender the transcript of the video that I had played because I read it onto the record two times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit those parts we saw this morning, including the part you showed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please, and I don't know if the practice would be to add them to the initial exhibit which was P6552, or mark it separately and then cross-reference it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't we include all these parts into Exhibit P6552. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the entire page meant or just the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those pages that we saw this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, the question was put to you here why you failed to say something in the statement. How was this statement created? Did you write it yourself or was it created in some other way?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An interview was conducted with me. I was told how to write, about what. I did it myself but I didn't do the typing. Somebody else did the typing. And perhaps carried away by the sentences and the meaning of the text, I did not pay attention to technical details such as dates, time, and perhaps even locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any questions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question related to - how shall I call that? - adjudicated facts in the second part, but the rest was up to me and to my vision to describe how I saw things, since it was not a dialogue but communication. Of course we corrected certain things to ensure that it was linguistically correct and followed a sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the cross-examination some things remained unclear regarding, in particular, your position and movements in the service along the chain of command. Do you remember when the operation at Jajce took place?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was September, towards the end of September. To answer this question, quite honestly, I would have to recall some facts because I was with my unit in a totally different theater of operations. The year was 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at 1D9629. It's somebody else's statement that I'm not going to tender, but we need to look at one detail in that statement. Can I see page 4, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Answering the question when you became the battalion commander, you said it was in the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was communicated to me in end August. Mr. President, please, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to clear up what I said about being and not being a commander, to make it perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were asked several times by Ms. Edgerton, and you wanted to clarify? Shall we collapse this document for the moment. Yes, please continue, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the establishment of my first war unit, I was put at the disposal of the municipality. Units were established because the earlier units ceased to operate, such as, for instance, the 13th Krajina Brigade that existed in peacetime, as reserve of course. So new units began to be established. The military database, the files were all mixed up so that people who worked in defence departments welcomed the idea of forming units based on information that was collected and lists that were made. When I got the offer to join the station, and it was all about regional replenishment of units, that is to say, the battalion was to be formed from the men in the Sanica area, initially - and I was proven right later - I refused. But it was a time when such behavior was not really popular. The president of the assembly and the president of the Council for National Defence, the officers from the municipality, had some understanding. And when I suggested that I should help establish the unit and train the officers and the men, they accepted pending a decision on my appointment as commander. And I believe that towards the end of August, one officer from the command came because a war assignment had already been given to the unit, and then I was told that I was appointed commander. And for understandable reasons, I could not refuse then. But to make it clearer, in the 17th Light Kljuc Brigade, I was -- until March 1993. And then I stayed for a while in Ostrelj at the headquarters of the 2nd Krajina Corps, and from there I was transferred to Grahovo municipality to be one of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish, Mr. President. In 1994 I was appointed from Grahovo to the war unit of the 2nd Engineering Regiment in Laniste. To be quite clear, these transfers took place according to the needs of service and the orders of the superior command. I ended the war in that unit. Now you can see my entire service during the war of which I am proud because I carried out my duties honourably and fully.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the fourth page again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you said you accepted to be appointed as a commander towards the end of August, did you mean the brigade or battalion? You accepted to be a commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, sorry. Commander of that battalion. I was never brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said you stayed in the 17th Light Kljuc Brigade until March 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 2nd Battalion was part of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. This is a statement given to the Muslim authorities by Borislav Jokic. Is the name familiar to you? He was captured somewhere and gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that man, particularly for the fact that he was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in the bottom paragraph: "As early as April 1992, the 1st Kljuc Battalion was established in Sitnica and Branko Ribic was appointed commander; whereas Captain Marko Ademovic was appointed assistant for morale guidance." What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was at Sitnica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I know they carried out these duties. I don't know if they were formally appointed to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between question and answer, in particular when you read something from the document. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further below, it says: "Until he left to go to war near Jajce, the 3rd Company was led by Captain Jovo Kevac ..." And then instead of him. Is this consistent with facts?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very clumsy interpretation because it was all about establishing the company that was part of that battalion. So I had the same duties as in Sanica. And the commander of that company which was not complete - it received additional recruits from the territory of Kljuc - eventually, their commander was Milovan Vojvodic. He was appointed to be their commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6543 is the next document I would like to show the witness. It's a contribution to the monograph of the 1st Krajina Corps. Second page, please -- sorry, third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much more do you need for your re-examination to be concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Maybe 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We better take a break now for 20 minutes. We will resume at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we just have the previous page to see whether that's the 2nd Battalion, the one that you talked about. The 2nd Infantry Battalion, did it grow out of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part. But there were also members who had not been members before or persons who had just moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, do they mention you at all in this initial period as battalion commander? Pekez, Gvozdenac, Mile Gajic, Mirko Markez, Milan Mitic, they are referred to.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with the municipality of Sipovo. I know this Captain Pekez.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. In English it is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you mentioned here as one of the officers in the first period?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 17th Kljuc, are you mentioned here at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This has to do with the 1st Battalion for the most part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8, please, in Serbian, and I think it's page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read this out to you: "The 2nd Infantry Battalion was deployed in the area of the village of Duljci and Gorica, and its task was to control the Jezero-Sipovo road and prevent the enemy from advancing in that area together with the forces located in the village of Duljci."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question that followed and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take a look at the transcript. Mr. Kevac, can you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this 2nd Battalion was from the municipality of Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of June, were you commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to me or to battalion commanders of other units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, were you one of the commanders at the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was still working on the establishment of the battalion in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 18843, that's the 65 ter number. Could that document please be shown to the witness. It seems that there is no translation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 18th of June. This is a combat report from the 17th Light Kljuc Brigade. And it says here: "During this reporting period in the area of responsibility of the brigade, no fire was opened by the Ustasha extremists." Number 2: "I decided" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's collapse this document. Yes, what is your question before putting this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether on the 18th of June he was in the corps command, whether he was part of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and here there is a reference to various persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered the question, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would like to have this document corroborate what he has been saying, because this commander is saying what he has available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 2 says --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very good. In what number? Only in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we put it on the ELMO. Yes, in the meantime you may continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can you tell us on the basis of this paragraph number 2: "I have decided to seal off, clear up, and search the terrain in order to force the remaining Ustasha forces to surrender unconditionally in the sector of Ljutica Brdo, Islamagici, Gornje Prhovo, and then to start searching the entire territory of the local communes of Humici and Peci in order to catch and liquidate the remaining Ustasha outlaws in this area." Could you please tell us what your role was at that time, if any, and also tell us whether this was regular military activity?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in this task, but I know that in Ljutica Brdo, because there is this hamlet, Ljutica Brdo, and then Veliki Litice is underneath, extremists stayed there for a long time and they really bothered both ethnic groups. These were legitimate military activities. A unit had been established and its only task was to capture these extremists and terrorists who had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that civilians and innocent persons would be involved in such activities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, how does this document relate to your question whether the witness was a battalion commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your Excellency, first I asked whether he took part in these activities. And then paragraph 3 - and I haven't even reached it yet - the commander is referring to the command corps and giving information about himself and another person called Ljubo Vracar, son of Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how is it related to your question, that whether the witness was a battalion commander at the time? You are just putting this document, leading the witness, and which doesn't seem to arise from the line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I asked him whether he became a commander and, if so, when. Now I am proffering evidence showing that he is not mentioned at all on the 18th of June as one of the commanders, and his statement is that he became a commander at the end of August. Along the way, he's been answering other questions, Prhovo, et cetera, all of these things were raised during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Karadzic, from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. But on page 6 of today's transcript, there is a reference to Prhovo, Pudin Han, in the question put by the Prosecution. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here on page 6, the question is: [In English] "So since you are not aware of these cases and since you told us yesterday you and your unit weren't there at the time, your comments in paragraph 15 to 22 of your statement about the events in Pudin Han and Prhovo are also just speculation; right?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this document related to that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the most important thing is that he was not mentioned as one of the commanders on the 18th of June. And then there is this other matter, namely, that Prhovo was a constant topic among the military, in terms of military activity, because it had been fortified and militarised. This is not speculation. These are generally known facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you've heard Dr. Karadzic's submission. We shall like very much to hear you in reply to that. Did I take you off guard?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I'm sorry. Slightly. I'm still trying to understand Dr. Karadzic's argument, and indeed that's why I'm slightly off guard because the witness confirmed that he's -- he wasn't in Prhovo, wasn't at Peci, and he's not aware of those cases. And the witness said that -- he confirmed that his answers were speculative. So I actually -- I'm frankly still at a loss to understand Dr. Karadzic's argument, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could try to help. I think what the point is here is was he the commander of the brigade at a certain time. The document that Dr. Karadzic has tried to -- has shown, according to Dr. Karadzic, would indicate -- would tend to indicate that he -- as at least the 18th of June he was not the brigade commander. Now, I have to admit that from looking at that document very quickly, I didn't catch why that document showed what Dr. Karadzic wants it to show. I didn't notice whether or not it reflected the list or a reference to all of the brigade commanders at the time. But to the extent that it does indicate that he was not a brigade commander at that time, that's the purpose for which it's being offered and I think that's both relevant and within the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been already reflected in the transcript; therefore, there is no need to admit this. Even if we are to admit it not for the content of the -- this document, only for the fact that he was not mentioned in this document. As such, I don't see any point of admitting it. So that's why I asked Mr. Karadzic to move on. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, these places that were enumerated, that the Prosecution suggested had been attacked as civilian locations, were they actually militarised; and in particular, can you tell us whether Biljani had been demilitarised, leaving aside the fact that no one is allowed to kill prisoners? Were these civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean Biljani, should I answer about that? In Biljani, as far as I can remember, five men or five uniforms were captured. I'm not sure now. I am referring to Muslims. All the rest were civilians, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1352, could that please be shown for a moment. This is already admitted. Can we show page 15 in Serbian and 9 in English, continuing on to page 10. The number is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at where it reads: "The units organised on the territorial principle, namely, Muslim units, Sehici one company; Rezevici, Egrlici, and then Biljani, three companies, around 200 men, Ale Mujazinovic [phoen] on the run."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. We collapse this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, maybe Dr. Karadzic could just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was what was the knowledge of the witness, whether Biljani was a demilitarised settlement or a militarised one, and he said that to the best of his recollection there were combatants over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he remembered five soldiers were captured, and then what's the point of showing this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well the point is, Excellencies, to see whether the settlements engaging in combat with the Serbian forces were civilian or whether there were armed forces among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you not put that question before putting the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did put that question before calling up the document. The witness said that he recalled that there were five prisoners taken, but I'm sure that this doesn't mean that there were only five of them. Not all of them were captured. My question was whether this was a militarised or a demilitarised area, whether they had units, why was there fighting going on, and why were individuals captured in Biljani? Excellencies, perhaps my line of questioning was not systemic but this is my last witness from Kljuc and I am not sure that I have dealt with the issue of Kljuc sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There are other Kljuc witnesses on the witness schedule, Mr. Jerosic [phoen] being one of them whose same we received yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't you put question one by one. So, for example, whether Kljuc or Biljani was militarised. Can you answer the question? Do you know whether or not Biljani was a militarised settlement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Muslims formed their own Territorial Defence and municipality and they had their staff at Velagici. According to the information that they didn't even try to conceal initially, it amounted to several battalions. The assumption at the time was that they had been formed on the basis of the territorial principle, which was only logical. I talked about those five men in a completely different time-frame. So on the whole, I don't think that that area was demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Prhovo, was it demilitarised or did it have an army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were extremists in Prhovo. They were a closed unit but had a special link with Ljutica hill, that was the area of Prhovo in the direction of the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many soldiers did these Muslim formations have in the municipality of Kljuc and all these various settlements?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we know that there were five to six battalions, that would be roughly 2.000 men. It depends. Did they have infantry units or light units? Of course, numbers would vary in that case. However, in view of the fact that the area was fragmented, I think that they were organised territorially and that, therefore, they had roughly 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, on the next page we can see that a figure is mentioned which is roughly the one stated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many residents of Kljuc were forwarded to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret that I don't have that information, Mr. President. I was simply not in Kljuc to be able to know this in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would direct the parties to pages 9 and 10 in English and 10 and 11 in Serbian where what the witness has just stated is discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
